Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.'}]

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, KD variants—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and using data-free or adversarial generation—enable trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Empirical and analytical work shows KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance, sometimes improve generalization, and enable deployment under privacy or resource constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. KD spans logits- and feature-based transfers, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and task-specific adaptations. Its strengths include enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, improving latency and memory footprints, and supporting privacy- or data-constrained scenarios. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, data availability and mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, architectural alignment, and deployment heterogeneity require complementary techniques and task-aware engineering to realize reliable, robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical set of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from larger or otherwise stronger models (teachers) to smaller or more constrained models (students). KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, speech, graph learning, reinforcement and lifelong learning—yielding work on algorithmic variants (self-distillation, multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial, relational and loss-function innovations), data- and privacy-aware designs, and hardware-aware/low-precision deployments. Empirical work demonstrates KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance, but theoretical and optimization limits remain: students often cannot perfectly match teachers and training/data choices matter greatly. Practical advances address these limits through better supervision signals, input-side design (data augmentation), alternate discrepancy measures, and privacy/communication constraints. The field continues to move toward more efficient, fair, private and domain-robust distilled models suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and sometimes improve robustness or task adaptation. A diverse toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and generative data-free techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and selective or meta-learned teaching—and empirical and theoretical work clarifies when and why these choices succeed or fail. Practical deployment requires matching the distilled signal to student capacity and task constraints, handling data- or architecture-mismatch, and explicitly addressing bias and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger systems. Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD methods vary by what is transferred (teacher logits, internal representations, attention, relational structure), how layers are aligned or projected, and how data constraints (limited access, privacy, or distribution shift) are handled. Empirical work demonstrates that combining output-level and representation-level objectives, using layer-mapping or projector modules, and adapting training data or curricula yields the best trade-offs between compactness and accuracy. Despite wide success, effective distillation requires careful choices about teacher quality, distilled signals, sample selection, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Power, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD variants transfer information via logits, intermediate features, or data synthesized from teachers; they can also be combined with privacy or fairness measures. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, dataset mismatches, and design choices (what to mimic, which layers, how to align teacher and student) strongly affect outcomes. Careful method selection—feature vs. logit supervision, layer alignment, projector usage, sample selection, and teacher adaptation—enables consistent gains while meeting constraints like limited data, privacy, or fairness.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Methods extend beyond simple teacher-logit matching to include feature and representation alignment, relational objectives, contrastive methods, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling, curriculum and progressive replacement schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware workflows. KD has been successfully applied across vision, language, speech, graph-structured data, retrieval, and constrained-device deployments, and is commonly combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency and memory budgets. Key practical concerns include what to transfer, how to cope with teacher-student mismatch and limited or private data, optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, and measurement of distilled model robustness and fairness. While empirical progress has been large and diverse, theoretical and systems-level problems remain active areas of research.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a logits-matching trick into a broad, practical framework for shrinking and adapting large models while retaining much of their performance. Modern KD techniques include soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, online and distributed formulations, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Across vision, language, recommendation, and domain-adaptation settings, KD is most effective when combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, pruning, quantization, curriculum or online training, and task-aware losses). Despite strong empirical successes, practitioners must attend to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and domain mismatch; many current research directions focus on robust, privacy-preserving, and data-limited distillation for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central approach for transferring behavior from large, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, more efficient models (students). Across modalities and tasks, KD is used both as a compression technique and as a means to inject inductive biases, stabilize continual learning, preserve privacy, and improve efficiency (compute, memory, latency) under deployment constraints. Practical KD pipelines combine logit-based supervision, intermediate-feature matching, architectural replacements, and training-time regularizers; they are often complemented with pruning, low-precision numerics, layer skipping, data augmentation, or specialized alignment strategies to handle mismatched inputs or modalities. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can capture “dark knowledge” beyond labels, transfer inductive biases, and sometimes enable students to outperform their teachers when paired with careful pre-training, data strategies, or architectural design. This synthesis summarizes techniques, motivations, and empirical patterns found in recent studies, and highlights open engineering considerations for applying KD in NLP, vision, graph, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performance deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across computer vision, generative modeling, 3D rendering, graph learning, and natural language processing, researchers employ a range of distillation paradigms — including teacher-student soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models — to produce smaller, faster, or more interpretable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. Practical concerns such as limited or unavailable training data, domain shifts, adversarial robustness, and the need for interpretable or low-precision models have driven specific adaptations of KD. Empirical results across tasks show that (1) distillation can greatly reduce model size or runtime with small accuracy loss, (2) internal- and feature-level matching often improves transfer beyond logits-only approaches, and (3) novel protocols (e.g., ensemble teachers, generative pseudo-replay, many-to-many layer alignment) expand KD applicability to privacy-sensitive, multimodal, and generation tasks.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Benefits, Practical Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD enables deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints, and can be adapted for task-specific compression, federated and data-free settings, low-precision inference, and bias- or domain-aware transfer. However, KD also carries practical limits: optimization gaps that prevent perfect teacher matching, transfer of teacher biases, failures on low-frequency phenomena, and sensitivity to data availability and teacher-student compatibility. To realize KD's promise practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, relations), consider multi-teacher and confidence-weighting schemes, leverage task-aware architecture search when appropriate, and adopt specialized strategies (data-free generation, reverse distillation, counterfactual augmentation, or federated protocols) to address specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across vision, generation, speech, and NLP tasks, distillation methods transfer logits, intermediate representations, and task-relevant signals; when combined with complementary compression techniques they enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Remaining practical challenges include selecting appropriate teacher signals, handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, and dealing with limited or private data, but a growing toolkit of task-aware, layer-wise, adversarial, and data-aware variants mitigates these issues.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies are now widespread across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation systems, and specialized settings (federated, few-shot, multi-modal, generative). Research has advanced along multiple axes: what to transfer (logits, features, attention, latent modules), how to shape the transfer (sample selection, adversarially-informed examples, curriculum, teacher ensembles, meta-learning), and special protocols for constrained environments (federated/black-box, few-shot, on-device inference). Empirical work shows KD can substantially close the performance gap between small and large models, enable practical deployment of generative and discriminative models, and, when extended, transfer robustness and interpretability. Remaining challenges include error propagation from teachers (especially for low-frequency phenomena), limitations under data heterogeneity in federated settings, and task-specific design choices for complex outputs (e.g., detection, segmentation, set outputs), motivating continued work on tailored distillation objectives and teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: What is known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression strategies form a broad, practically driven toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, graph learning, self-supervision, and reinforcement learning—research has developed many algorithmic variants (logit and feature matching, attention/relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes), system-level protocols (federated, black-box, data-free), and architecture-aware methods (task-adaptive compression, neural architecture search, pruning and quantization combinations). Empirically, KD often substantially reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success depends on teacher–student alignment, available data and augmentations, and task-specific design; remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, domain shift, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Practical deployments balance distilled signals, data strategies, and architecture choices to achieve required trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, widely used toolbox to transfer behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, resource-efficient students. The approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or generated samples), whether original training data are available, and whether the objective emphasizes efficiency, privacy, robustness, or interpretability. Across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives and training pipelines—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—produce compact models that approach teacher performance under deployment constraints. Key practical challenges are capacity and optimization mismatch between teacher and student, data- and privacy-limited settings, distribution shift and low-frequency phenomena, and the risk of transferring undesirable teacher traits; promising responses include task-aware filtering of teacher signals, multi-layer mapping strategies, data-free sample synthesis, and privacy-preserving noise mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Directions (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, ensemble, or otherwise specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment-ready student models. KD techniques operate at different supervision granularities (soft-labels, intermediate representations, relational or attention maps, adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings) and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis to meet latency, memory, privacy, or heterogeneity constraints. Across modalities—NLP, vision, speech, graph learning, generation, and reinforcement learning—KD has enabled large reductions in model size and runtime with modest performance loss and has been adapted for settings without access to original training data, for federated or continual learning, and for transferring inductive biases. Important practical challenges remain (teacher selection and adaptation, data availability and distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, bias transfer, and privacy), and current best practices emphasize carefully matched teacher-student design, auxiliary training signals, and integration with other compression tools to achieve reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Work across vision, generative modeling, reinforcement learning, recommendation, and language has developed diverse objectives and mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, adversarial synthesis of training data, multi-teacher/ensemble supervision, layer-wise and task-adaptive compression, and data-augmentation-enhanced distillation. These approaches trade off accuracy, inference cost, and robustness and address practical constraints such as lack of access to original training data, domain shift, fairness, and heterogeneous model architectures. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or sometimes match teacher performance while substantially reducing FLOPs, parameters, or latency, but limitations remain in data heterogeneity, low-frequency token transfer, and privacy-constrained settings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, applications, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers, ensembles, or supernets) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, distillation strategies include matching logits, mimicking intermediate features, adversarial generation of surrogate data, ensemble compression, and teacher-student co-training. Practical extensions address limited or private data, multi-teacher and domain-shift scenarios, and architecture search for generative models. Empirical results show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, pretraining of compact models, and task-aware feature imitation can preserve much of the teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, and that specialized methods are required for structured outputs (e.g., detection, segmentation, ranking) and domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative modeling, researchers transfer information via softened output distributions, intermediate-feature matching, relational and attention maps, and many-to-many layer alignment. Variants address resource heterogeneity, data unavailability, privacy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical and analytic work shows that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, but its success depends on design choices (what to transfer, teacher quality, data or pseudo-data, and alignment losses). State-of-the-art practice mixes logits-based loss with feature- or representation-level objectives, task-aware augmentations, and architecture- or training-aware modifications to obtain favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core method for producing compact, efficient models from large deep networks across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD delivers substantial inference and memory savings while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, enabling deployment in latency-, power-, and privacy-constrained settings. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections (biases, distributional blind spots) and faces practical constraints (data mismatch, teacher–student capacity gaps, limited-data regimes). Effective use of KD therefore requires matching objectives, data strategies, and architectures to deployment goals and complementing distillation with pruning, quantization, or privacy-aware protocols when necessary.
