papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are no longer just ways to reduce parameter counts; when designed thoughtfully they preserve or even improve task performance, domain robustness, and privacy while enabling real-time deployment. Effective distillation requires going beyond matching output probabilities: transferring internal representations, using task- and domain-aware selection of teacher signals, leveraging ensemble or adversarial schemes when appropriate, and adopting data-aware or data-free augmentation techniques. In application domains from NLP to vision, multi-modal systems, and graph learning, tailored distillation strategies yield substantial speedups and parameter reductions with minimal loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy. This paper synthesizes evidence across diverse recent works to advocate a principled, task-centered approach to distillation and compression.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Pragmatic, Multifaceted Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a multifaceted framework—covering logits, intermediate representations, feature maps, sample selection, and data-side interventions—KD enables deployments under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a broadly useful means to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students so that compressed models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is adapted to the problem: what to transfer (logits, features, attention), which data to use or synthesize, how to weight multiple teachers or imperfect supervision, and how to integrate complementary compression techniques. However, KD is neither automatic nor sufficient on its own: careful, task-aware design and combination with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies are required to realize reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. The literature converges on a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure, decision-boundary samples), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, teacher-annealing, self- or online-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data approaches), and architecture-aware adaptations (many-to-many layer mapping, projector adapters, and combinations with pruning/quantization). Empirical studies across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and generative tasks show distilled students can recover much teacher performance and sometimes yield superior efficiency–accuracy trade-offs; nonetheless, open problems remain around data scarcity and privacy, teacher–student mismatch, preserving low-frequency behaviors, and transferring robustness and fairness properties.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. KD spans logits- and feature-based transfers, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and task-specific adaptations. Its strengths include enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, improving latency and memory footprints, and supporting privacy- or data-constrained scenarios. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, data availability and mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, architectural alignment, and deployment heterogeneity require complementary techniques and task-aware engineering to realize reliable, robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, KD variants—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and using data-free or adversarial generation—enable trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Empirical and analytical work shows KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance, sometimes improve generalization, and enable deployment under privacy or resource constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Multifaceted Argument for Responsible Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students that retain much of the teacher's performance. KD has been extended beyond simple logit matching to transfer intermediate representations, channel- or attention-level signals, ranking and relational knowledge, and to operate in data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings. When combined with complementary compression techniques and careful training protocols, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and domain constraints; however, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their capabilities. KD enables deployment across modalities and constrained environments, and empirical work shows it can approach teacher performance when combined with complementary techniques. However, KD is not a universal solution: it can propagate teacher errors and biases, struggle under data scarcity or mismatch, and require careful choices of distilled targets, architectures, and training schedules. To realize KD's benefits in production and research settings, practitioners should pair distillation with targeted remedies—representation-aware objectives, data-and-curriculum strategies, ensemble or adversarial schemes, and fairness or privacy interventions—tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and federated settings, KD variants transfer soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, contrastive signals, synthetic inputs, or ensemble outputs. KD can enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, improve student generalization, support privacy-preserving workflows, and interact fruitfully with pruning and low-precision numerics. However, the benefits depend strongly on data availability, teacher quality, architecture alignment, and training protocols; important failure modes include optimization gaps, preserved or amplified teacher biases, degraded rare-token behavior, and teacher inference cost. The literature provides many practical strategies—feature- and layer-wise matching, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial or data-free sample generation, student-aware teacher design, and hardware-aware co-design—to mitigate these limitations and extend KD to specialized tasks such as federated learning, continual/lifelong learning, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from large, expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, efficient models. Methods include logit-based distillation, feature- or representation-based matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving approaches, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. KD has been applied across modalities and domains—vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, generative models, and healthcare—demonstrating gains in inference efficiency, robustness, generalization, and interpretability when appropriately designed. Open challenges remain around data availability, teacher–student mismatch, selection of distilled signals and samples, and principled integration with other compression techniques; recent work proposes meta-learning teachers, adaptive teacher weighting, projector modules, and task-adaptive compression as practical remedies.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behaviors and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, graph, and federated settings, KD variants—ranging from logit-based soft-label transfer to feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and ensemble or multi-teacher approaches—have enabled deployment on constrained devices, improved inference latency, and supported privacy- and domain-aware workflows. Practical deployment mixes KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-conditioning strategies; however, limitations remain around teacher–student mismatches, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data availability, and optimization stability. The literature proposes targeted remedies (attention-based layer mapping, student-friendly teacher training, few-shot and zero-shot approaches, and federated KD protocols) and points toward continued work on principled teacher design, privacy guarantees, hardware-aware objectives, and robust distillation for low-resource regimes.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, distillation is used to transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger, more accurate teachers to smaller, faster students; it also appears within automated model search, pruning and distributed training workflows. Work in this area spans logit matching, representation-level objectives, data-free and few-shot regimes, multi-/online-teacher schemes, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy while enabling large reductions in memory and compute, but limitations remain around optimization, data availability, and the preservation or mitigation of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports privacy-aware and data-limited settings, and generalizes across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models). However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and complementary engineering (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and training pipelines). Reliable, high-quality compression therefore treats distillation as a core technique within a broader, task-aware compression strategy rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger systems. Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher-to-student logit-matching recipe into a diverse toolkit that addresses compression, cross-model transfer, domain adaptation, privacy, and deployment constraints. Across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains, methods that transfer internal representations, align features across layers, leverage adversarial or boundary-focused samples, or synthesize distilled training data enable smaller models to approximate or even match larger models on task performance while meeting latency, fairness, and interpretability demands. Effective use of KD depends on matching the distillation paradigm to the target problem: use internal/feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP tasks, layer- and task-aware filters when capacity mismatch is large, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling to improve generalization, and data-free or federated-aware strategies when data access is restricted. Combining KD with pruning and hardware-aware compression further increases suitability for edge deployment.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and powerful approach for compressing models across modalities, but its effectiveness depends on design choices spanning what is distilled (logits, features, internal representations), how inputs are prepared (augmentation, sample selection), how multiple teachers are reconciled, and whether robustness or task-specific structure is considered. Recent work shows that combining soft-target regularization with feature- and intermediate-representation matching, careful input-side interventions, and adaptive distillation objectives yields the best tradeoffs between compression, accuracy, and robustness across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative-model settings.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable models across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When paired with complementary techniques—layer mapping, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, pruning/quantization, and curriculum or online schemes—KD yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance while supporting privacy-conscious and latency-constrained deployments. Remaining limits around data availability, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional mismatch can be mitigated by choosing appropriate distillation targets and architectures and by combining KD with targeted engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the capabilities of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so that students achieve improved accuracy, latency, or resource use while retaining much of teacher behavior. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, internal features, relational structure, or contrastive/global representations), how supervision is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and how distillation is combined with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows substantial gains across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and generative models, but limitations remain around data availability, teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency information transfer, privacy constraints, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their capabilities. KD enables deployment across modalities and constrained environments, and empirical work shows it can approach teacher performance when combined with complementary techniques. However, KD is not a universal solution: it can propagate teacher errors and biases, struggle under data scarcity or mismatch, and require careful choices of distilled targets, architectures, and training schedules. To realize KD's benefits in production and research settings, practitioners should pair distillation with targeted remedies—representation-aware objectives, data-and-curriculum strategies, ensemble or adversarial schemes, and fairness or privacy interventions—tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Universal Tool for Model Compression and Practical Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique that enables model compression, deployment efficiency, and task- or domain-specific adaptation across a wide range of deep learning settings. Empirical work shows KD can reduce memory and compute with small accuracy loss, enable low-precision inference, compress specialized generative or multi-modal models, and provide routes to interpretability and data- or privacy-constrained scenarios. Best results arise when KD is adapted to the task (choice of objectives, teacher ensembles, data augmentation, or data-free strategies) and when student architectures or training protocols explicitly account for heterogeneity between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers capabilities of large models into smaller ones via indirect supervision. Methods vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and practical constraints (limited data, privacy, cross-distribution generalization, modality mismatch). Empirical work across speech, vision, language, retrieval, graph, generative modeling, and medical imaging shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while gaining resource efficiency; theoretical analyses and diagnostic studies clarify mechanisms and guide designs such as projector layers, many-to-many layer mapping, and curriculum or data-augmentation strategies. Remaining challenges include distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of inductive biases, and principled layer-to-layer alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.
