papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Riley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge from high-capacity teachers to compact students across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based recipes into feature- and layer-level matching, many-to-many layer mappings, self-supervised distillation, data-free and online KD, task- and domain-adaptive compression, and combinations with architecture search and low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs involving teacher quality, the role of soft targets as regularizers, and practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, and inference latency. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical patterns, and open directions drawn from the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade these techniques have diversified from simple logit-matching to a broad set of objectives and pipelines — including feature- and representation-matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial procedures, data-free and privacy-aware methods, multi-teacher schemes, teacher design, and selective sample strategies. KD has been applied across domains (NLP, vision, graph learning, generative models, novel-view synthesis, speech, and recommender systems), producing substantial reductions in parameters and latency while retaining or sometimes improving downstream performance. The literature highlights important practical trade-offs (utility vs. fairness, robustness, data availability, and teacher–student mismatch), and suggests promising directions in adaptive teacher design, rigorous uncertainty and fairness controls, and domain- and task-specific distillation objectives.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression trick into a broad set of techniques that enable efficient deployment, cross-modal transfer, federated and privacy-preserving learning, and improved generalization across domains. Empirical results across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs) show that KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining most of the teacher performance. However, the success of KD depends on careful choices — teacher quality, what to distill (outputs, features, internal representations), data availability and augmentation, and the loss or alignment mechanism — and recent work proposes multiple refinements (multi-teacher schemes, adversarial critics, projector modules, teacher-free variants) that mitigate known failure modes. The balance of empirical evidence and theoretical analyses indicates that KD is both practically indispensable for many compression tasks and a fertile area for research on how knowledge should be measured, transferred, and regularized.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical and flexible pathway to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across NLP and other modalities, researchers have developed logit-level, representation-level, layer-wise, multi-teacher, data-free, privacy-aware, and task-aware distillation variants and combined KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and low-frequency phenomena materially affects student quality and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have evolved from a simple teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a broad toolbox for producing compact, efficient, and adaptable models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research has produced a range of practical methods—logit and feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware variants, and federated or online protocols—and has clarified connections to regularization, ensemble learning, and optimization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of the teacher's performance, though gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and adaptation to deployment constraints. This synthesis summarizes core methods, theoretical insights, empirical findings, practical considerations, and open challenges that shape current best practice for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. Major limitations remain in imperfect belief matching, distribution shift, handling low-frequency phenomena, heterogeneous or privacy-constrained data, and principled teacher selection—areas where methodological and theoretical progress continues to be needed.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger or ensemble teachers. It supports a wide range of objectives—logit-level transfer, feature- and representation-level matching, relational and adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings—and is applicable across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models) and settings (offline, online, data-free, federated, multi-teacher). When combined with careful teacher-student co-design, targeted data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while also serving secondary goals such as interpretability or robustness. KD is powerful but not automatic: success depends on matching objectives to tasks, mitigating teacher-induced errors or biases, and addressing optimization and data-distribution challenges.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Power, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD variants transfer information via logits, intermediate features, or data synthesized from teachers; they can also be combined with privacy or fairness measures. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, dataset mismatches, and design choices (what to mimic, which layers, how to align teacher and student) strongly affect outcomes. Careful method selection—feature vs. logit supervision, layer alignment, projector usage, sample selection, and teacher adaptation—enables consistent gains while meeting constraints like limited data, privacy, or fairness.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When adapted to task, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprint, and improved adaptability across domains and modalities. However, KD is a family of techniques rather than a single algorithm: best outcomes arise from combining distillation with complementary methods (e.g., pruning, architecture search, curriculum design, data synthesis) and from explicitly addressing challenges such as imperfect teachers, domain shift, privacy, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment across domains and modalities. When designed with task-awareness (choice of distilled signal, teacher selection, and training scheme), KD can preserve accuracy while materially improving latency, memory, and privacy characteristics. Best results arise from combining multiple KD techniques (logit, feature, layer-wise, adversarial, and ensemble-based) chosen to match the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become core methods for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers across computer vision, speech, graph-based learning, and NLP. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based teacher-student paradigm into feature- and representation-based distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, online and adversarial schemes, and task-specific adaptations (e.g., for BERT and non-autoregressive translation). Work also addresses robustness, privacy, few-shot compression, and practical efficiency (reduced compute and communication) for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Power, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD variants transfer information via logits, intermediate features, or data synthesized from teachers; they can also be combined with privacy or fairness measures. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, dataset mismatches, and design choices (what to mimic, which layers, how to align teacher and student) strongly affect outcomes. Careful method selection—feature vs. logit supervision, layer alignment, projector usage, sample selection, and teacher adaptation—enables consistent gains while meeting constraints like limited data, privacy, or fairness.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, distillation is used to transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger, more accurate teachers to smaller, faster students; it also appears within automated model search, pruning and distributed training workflows. Work in this area spans logit matching, representation-level objectives, data-free and few-shot regimes, multi-/online-teacher schemes, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy while enabling large reductions in memory and compute, but limitations remain around optimization, data availability, and the preservation or mitigation of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Pragmatic, Multifaceted Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a multifaceted framework—covering logits, intermediate representations, feature maps, sample selection, and data-side interventions—KD enables deployments under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.
