papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical Tool That Requires Context-Aware Integration
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable technique for transferring behavior from large teacher models to compact students across vision, language, generative, and distributed settings. However, KD is not a silver bullet; its success depends on teacher quality, choice of distilled signals, available data, and optimization procedures. For practical, high-fidelity compression, KD should be treated as a core component of a broader pipeline that includes pre-training of compact architectures, careful layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher or meta-learned teaching strategies, data-aware augmentation or synthesis, and complementary compression methods such as pruning or quantization.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a flexible set of techniques to compress large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, generative modeling, and structured prediction domains, KD variants — including logit transfer, feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free distillation, and task-specific adaptations — provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, low-precision numerics, pruning and layer skipping, or teacher training tailored to students, distillation yields practical, deployable models applicable to constrained hardware and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad toolbox for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models to smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving models. Methods range from soft-logit supervision to internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, NLP, graphs, and federated settings shows KD can recover much of a teacher's performance in resource-constrained deployments, while challenges remain in teacher selection, data availability, bias propagation, and task-specific design.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Benefits, Practical Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD enables deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints, and can be adapted for task-specific compression, federated and data-free settings, low-precision inference, and bias- or domain-aware transfer. However, KD also carries practical limits: optimization gaps that prevent perfect teacher matching, transfer of teacher biases, failures on low-frequency phenomena, and sensitivity to data availability and teacher-student compatibility. To realize KD's promise practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, relations), consider multi-teacher and confidence-weighting schemes, leverage task-aware architecture search when appropriate, and adopt specialized strategies (data-free generation, reverse distillation, counterfactual augmentation, or federated protocols) to address specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core set of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and layer correspondences; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search. KD supports many practical settings — including data-limited, data-free, few-shot, federated, and cross-modal scenarios — but its effectiveness depends on choices such as which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Ongoing directions include principled theory for transfer objectives, robust and private distillation, and task-aware designs for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques that make large, high-performing models practical for deployment by transferring behavior, representations, or decision structure to smaller models. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when combined with appropriate supervision signals, data practices, and architectural alignment, but it also has important failure modes—propagated teacher errors, sensitivity to data distribution and teacher quality, and limits when student capacity is insufficient. I argue KD should be treated as a foundational component of model-compression pipelines, applied thoughtfully and in combination with complementary methods (augmentation, pruning/quantization, privacy mechanisms, and federated protocols) to realize robust, efficient systems for real-world NLP and deep-learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking model size and latency while preserving performance across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation, and federated settings. Research has expanded beyond the original logits-matching paradigm into feature mimicking, many-to-many layer mapping, teacher engineering, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights important interactions between data complexity, teacher strength, inductive bias, and augmentation strategies, and identifies practical challenges including model-heterogeneity, data heterogeneity, and the need for robust data-free methods. The field increasingly emphasizes not only how to distill but also what to distill (logits, features, inter-class relations, view- or task-specific knowledge) and how to adapt distillation to application constraints (privacy, federated settings, domain shifts, resource budgets).

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports privacy-aware and data-limited settings, and generalizes across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models). However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and complementary engineering (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and training pipelines). Reliable, high-quality compression therefore treats distillation as a core technique within a broader, task-aware compression strategy rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis reviews empirical and methodological advances in knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques as applied across vision, language, generative models, retrieval, recommender systems, federated and lifelong learning. It summarizes mechanisms for transferring teacher knowledge to smaller students (soft labels, intermediate representations, curriculum and selective sample strategies), practical challenges (data availability, teacher cost, domain shift, privacy, and bias), and targeted solutions (data-free distillation, fast label generation, multi-teacher and domain-adaptive schemes, self-distillation, and distillation-aware pruning). The goal is to map what the provided literature reports about when distillation helps, when it can hurt, and which strategies are effective for different settings and tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Power, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD variants transfer information via logits, intermediate features, or data synthesized from teachers; they can also be combined with privacy or fairness measures. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, dataset mismatches, and design choices (what to mimic, which layers, how to align teacher and student) strongly affect outcomes. Careful method selection—feature vs. logit supervision, layer alignment, projector usage, sample selection, and teacher adaptation—enables consistent gains while meeting constraints like limited data, privacy, or fairness.
