papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger systems. Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade these techniques have diversified from simple logit-matching to a broad set of objectives and pipelines — including feature- and representation-matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial procedures, data-free and privacy-aware methods, multi-teacher schemes, teacher design, and selective sample strategies. KD has been applied across domains (NLP, vision, graph learning, generative models, novel-view synthesis, speech, and recommender systems), producing substantial reductions in parameters and latency while retaining or sometimes improving downstream performance. The literature highlights important practical trade-offs (utility vs. fairness, robustness, data availability, and teacher–student mismatch), and suggests promising directions in adaptive teacher design, rigorous uncertainty and fairness controls, and domain- and task-specific distillation objectives.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and federated settings, KD variants transfer soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, contrastive signals, synthetic inputs, or ensemble outputs. KD can enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, improve student generalization, support privacy-preserving workflows, and interact fruitfully with pruning and low-precision numerics. However, the benefits depend strongly on data availability, teacher quality, architecture alignment, and training protocols; important failure modes include optimization gaps, preserved or amplified teacher biases, degraded rare-token behavior, and teacher inference cost. The literature provides many practical strategies—feature- and layer-wise matching, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial or data-free sample generation, student-aware teacher design, and hardware-aware co-design—to mitigate these limitations and extend KD to specialized tasks such as federated learning, continual/lifelong learning, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Yet Contextual, Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has repeatedly enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across modalities while retaining much of the performance of larger models. Empirical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, inductive biases, and task-specific capabilities from teacher to student, and can be adapted via logit-, feature-, and layer-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial procedures, and data- or privacy-aware variants. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization difficulties, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and propagation of teacher errors limit its effectiveness unless combined with careful protocol design and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as a first-class tool in compression toolkits, but only when used with task-aware filtering, capacity-aware targets, and architecture- or data-aware refinements to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring information from large, often multi-modal or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD has been adapted into many forms — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and offline protocols, and data-free or zero-shot schemes — and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance in many settings when teacher quality, student capacity, and appropriate data or synthesis strategies are addressed; theoretical and empirical analyses highlight KD’s role both as knowledge transfer and as a regularizer. Despite broad success, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or heterogeneous data, and propagation of teacher artifacts; current best practice is to treat KD as one element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving—sometimes even improving—task performance. Methods operate at the level of logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision boundaries and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and federated or data-free workflows. Practical deployments require careful alignment of teacher and student inputs and objectives, attention to data availability and privacy, and strategies for dealing with capacity gaps and distributional heterogeneity. Across vision, language, speech, recommender, and multimodal tasks, tailored distillation pipelines enable compact models suitable for resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and federative settings, distillation can preserve much of a teacher's predictive quality while reducing inference latency, memory footprint, and communication costs. Different distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, contrastive signals) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot) make KD adaptable to diverse deployment constraints. At the same time, distillation has well-documented failure modes—transfer of teacher biases, degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena, sensitivity to data heterogeneity and teacher–student capacity mismatch—and practical success depends on task-aware design choices and often combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. The field thus treats KD as a multifaceted, application-driven set of methods whose best practice is to match signals, data, and student capacity to deployment needs while applying targeted mitigations for privacy, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Is a Core Tool for Model Compression and Efficient NLP/Deep Learning Systems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile technique for producing compact, fast, and privacy-aware models across modalities. KD not only compresses large pretrained models for low-latency deployment, but also enables domain adaptation, federated and data-free scenarios, continual learning, and improved student generalization when combined with feature-level and architectural interventions. Together, methodological advances—ranging from feature mimicking and projector ensembles to student-friendly teachers and adversarial/data-free generation—make KD an essential component of modern model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD encompasses logits-based, feature- and representation-level, multi-teacher, online, self-distillation, and privacy-aware variants, and its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and integrating complementary compression and training practices. When combined with architecture-aware design, augmentation or synthetic-data generation, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols, KD enables deployable models across resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. Major limitations remain in imperfect belief matching, distribution shift, handling low-frequency phenomena, heterogeneous or privacy-constrained data, and principled teacher selection—areas where methodological and theoretical progress continues to be needed.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and powerful approach for compressing models across modalities, but its effectiveness depends on design choices spanning what is distilled (logits, features, internal representations), how inputs are prepared (augmentation, sample selection), how multiple teachers are reconciled, and whether robustness or task-specific structure is considered. Recent work shows that combining soft-target regularization with feature- and intermediate-representation matching, careful input-side interventions, and adaptive distillation objectives yields the best tradeoffs between compression, accuracy, and robustness across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative-model settings.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Multifaceted Argument for Responsible Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students that retain much of the teacher's performance. KD has been extended beyond simple logit matching to transfer intermediate representations, channel- or attention-level signals, ranking and relational knowledge, and to operate in data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings. When combined with complementary compression techniques and careful training protocols, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and domain constraints; however, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a central, practical toolkit for shrinking large neural models while preserving functionality for deployment, adaptation, and efficiency in deep learning and natural language processing. Research has developed a broad set of distillation objectives and training protocols, applied these techniques across modalities and structured tasks, and integrated KD with complementary compression methods. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance and enable new use cases (on-device inference, privacy-aware releases, multi-teacher ensembles, and task adaptation), while ongoing challenges include teacher imperfection, data heterogeneity, transferring fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, and principled guarantees for fairness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic for compressing neural networks into a broad, practically validated family of techniques for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD methods transfer information via outputs, intermediate features, relational signals, or synthesized data, and they are applied across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, multimodal) and problem classes (classification, detection, generation, reinforcement learning, segmentation, view synthesis). Practical success depends on matching the distillation strategy to the task and deployment constraints (data availability, privacy, capacity, latency, hardware), and on integrating KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware adaptations. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfections, capacity mismatch, limited or private data, and preserving rare-token or low-frequency behaviour in sequence models.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Benefits, Practical Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD enables deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints, and can be adapted for task-specific compression, federated and data-free settings, low-precision inference, and bias- or domain-aware transfer. However, KD also carries practical limits: optimization gaps that prevent perfect teacher matching, transfer of teacher biases, failures on low-frequency phenomena, and sensitivity to data availability and teacher-student compatibility. To realize KD's promise practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, relations), consider multi-teacher and confidence-weighting schemes, leverage task-aware architecture search when appropriate, and adopt specialized strategies (data-free generation, reverse distillation, counterfactual augmentation, or federated protocols) to address specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. Methods span soft-label supervision, feature- and layer-wise imitation, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but gains depend strongly on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, domain shift, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behaviors and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, graph, and federated settings, KD variants—ranging from logit-based soft-label transfer to feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and ensemble or multi-teacher approaches—have enabled deployment on constrained devices, improved inference latency, and supported privacy- and domain-aware workflows. Practical deployment mixes KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-conditioning strategies; however, limitations remain around teacher–student mismatches, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data availability, and optimization stability. The literature proposes targeted remedies (attention-based layer mapping, student-friendly teacher training, few-shot and zero-shot approaches, and federated KD protocols) and points toward continued work on principled teacher design, privacy guarantees, hardware-aware objectives, and robust distillation for low-resource regimes.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for compressing large models and transferring capabilities across domains, modalities, and architectures. When combined with task-aware objectives, careful layer/feature matching, and appropriate data or privacy strategies, KD yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment patterns. KD’s strengths span supervised, self-supervised, online, and privacy-constrained settings, but realizing them requires attention to teacher quality, what knowledge is transferred, and how student capacity and data constraints are handled.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Hamilton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to the task, available data, and student capacity, KD can deliver substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving most of the teacher's performance. Success depends on selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, annealing), and how to handle limited or private data (data-free synthesis, adversarial generators, teacher-free regularizers). Although KD is broadly effective, it is not a panacea: failures arise from teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, optimization issues, and transferred biases, motivating targeted protocols and continued research into privacy-aware, robust, and automated distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Work across vision, generative modeling, reinforcement learning, recommendation, and language has developed diverse objectives and mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, adversarial synthesis of training data, multi-teacher/ensemble supervision, layer-wise and task-adaptive compression, and data-augmentation-enhanced distillation. These approaches trade off accuracy, inference cost, and robustness and address practical constraints such as lack of access to original training data, domain shift, fairness, and heterogeneous model architectures. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or sometimes match teacher performance while substantially reducing FLOPs, parameters, or latency, but limitations remain in data heterogeneity, low-frequency token transfer, and privacy-constrained settings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, applications, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but computationally expensive neural networks in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more specialized ones. This synthesis summarizes methods for transferring output-level and internal representations, architectural and layer-wise strategies for compression, training variants (e.g., self-supervised, adversarial, few-shot, online, and federated settings), and applications across NLP, vision, generative models, graph learning, and distributed systems. It highlights empirical findings on when distillation is most effective, techniques to preserve or improve robustness and fairness, and practical strategies for heterogeneous and latency-sensitive deployments. Gaps and recurring challenges are identified to guide future work.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central approach for transferring behavior from large, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, more efficient models (students). Across modalities and tasks, KD is used both as a compression technique and as a means to inject inductive biases, stabilize continual learning, preserve privacy, and improve efficiency (compute, memory, latency) under deployment constraints. Practical KD pipelines combine logit-based supervision, intermediate-feature matching, architectural replacements, and training-time regularizers; they are often complemented with pruning, low-precision numerics, layer skipping, data augmentation, or specialized alignment strategies to handle mismatched inputs or modalities. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can capture “dark knowledge” beyond labels, transfer inductive biases, and sometimes enable students to outperform their teachers when paired with careful pre-training, data strategies, or architectural design. This synthesis summarizes techniques, motivations, and empirical patterns found in recent studies, and highlights open engineering considerations for applying KD in NLP, vision, graph, and multimodal systems.
