papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable models across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When paired with complementary techniques—layer mapping, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, pruning/quantization, and curriculum or online schemes—KD yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance while supporting privacy-conscious and latency-constrained deployments. Remaining limits around data availability, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional mismatch can be mitigated by choosing appropriate distillation targets and architectures and by combining KD with targeted engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher–student soft-label transfer into a flexible set of methods that enable compact, fast, and often more robust models across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings. When designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and deployment demands, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, layer skipping, meta-learned teachers, or generative replay) reliably yields practical gains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to preserve robustness and fairness. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in compression pipelines: powerful and broadly applicable when paired with principled, task-centered decisions, but demand-aware and tuned to deployment objectives.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When adapted to task, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprint, and improved adaptability across domains and modalities. However, KD is a family of techniques rather than a single algorithm: best outcomes arise from combining distillation with complementary methods (e.g., pruning, architecture search, curriculum design, data synthesis) and from explicitly addressing challenges such as imperfect teachers, domain shift, privacy, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled Toolbox for Practical and Responsible Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that can produce compact, deployable models when combined with complementary design choices. Properly applied—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to map layers, and which auxiliary techniques to use (pretraining, curriculum, adversarial or privacy safeguards)—KD can deliver students that approach or sometimes match teacher performance while enabling latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (data heterogeneity, low-frequency phenomena, imperfect teachers, and optimization challenges) that demand targeted mitigations rather than blind application.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while enabling adaptation across tasks, domains, and modalities. When combined with representation-level objectives, careful teacher engineering, pre-training of compact architectures, and input-side interventions (e.g., augmentation or data synthesis), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss and can enable deployment under tight compute, latency, or privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is not a single recipe: success depends on optimization choices, teacher–student alignment, and dataset properties, which motivates tailored distillation objectives, data strategies, and evaluation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are now core tools for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. The literature has expanded far beyond simple logits matching to include feature- and representation-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, and tight integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates broad applicability across modalities (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and generative models) and deployment contexts (edge devices, federated systems, and data-constrained settings). The main practical challenges are (1) choosing what and how to distill for a given task and student architecture, (2) coping with limited or unavailable original training data, (3) avoiding transfer of teacher weaknesses (e.g., biases or low-frequency degradation), and (4) co-designing distillation with other compression primitives and hardware constraints. Progress comes from combining representational objectives, layer-mapping strategies, task-aware teacher selection, and safeguards (privacy or fairness) appropriate to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade these techniques have diversified from simple logit-matching to a broad set of objectives and pipelines — including feature- and representation-matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial procedures, data-free and privacy-aware methods, multi-teacher schemes, teacher design, and selective sample strategies. KD has been applied across domains (NLP, vision, graph learning, generative models, novel-view synthesis, speech, and recommender systems), producing substantial reductions in parameters and latency while retaining or sometimes improving downstream performance. The literature highlights important practical trade-offs (utility vs. fairness, robustness, data availability, and teacher–student mismatch), and suggests promising directions in adaptive teacher design, rigorous uncertainty and fairness controls, and domain- and task-specific distillation objectives.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Multifaceted Argument for Responsible Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students that retain much of the teacher's performance. KD has been extended beyond simple logit matching to transfer intermediate representations, channel- or attention-level signals, ranking and relational knowledge, and to operate in data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings. When combined with complementary compression techniques and careful training protocols, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and domain constraints; however, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a pragmatic pathway to compress large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Empirical work across vision, speech, language, multimodal and graph domains shows KD can retain much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory when combined with complementary compression tools. However, real-world success requires careful choice of teacher signals, data strategies, and optimization protocols to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and modality or deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the capabilities of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Directions (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, ensemble, or otherwise specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment-ready student models. KD techniques operate at different supervision granularities (soft-labels, intermediate representations, relational or attention maps, adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings) and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis to meet latency, memory, privacy, or heterogeneity constraints. Across modalities—NLP, vision, speech, graph learning, generation, and reinforcement learning—KD has enabled large reductions in model size and runtime with modest performance loss and has been adapted for settings without access to original training data, for federated or continual learning, and for transferring inductive biases. Important practical challenges remain (teacher selection and adaptation, data availability and distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, bias transfer, and privacy), and current best practices emphasize carefully matched teacher-student design, auxiliary training signals, and integration with other compression tools to achieve reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster ones while transferring performance and often additional properties such as robustness or cross-domain adaptability. Evidence across vision, language, graph, and sequential domains shows KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained settings, supports continual and federated learning, and can be combined with pruning, architecture search, and adversarial strategies. However, distillation is not a universal panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, interact nontrivially with regularization strategies, and requires careful alignment of inputs, representations, and objectives. Best practice is to treat KD as a family of tools (logit, intermediate-layer, feature, adversarial, data-driven, self-distillation) and to adapt the distillation design to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.'}, {'author': 'Henson', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems."}, {'author': 'Freeman', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Directions (Synthesis)', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, ensemble, or otherwise specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment-ready student models. Across modalities—NLP, vision, speech, graph learning, generation, and reinforcement learning—KD has enabled large reductions in model size and runtime with modest performance loss and has been adapted for settings without access to original training data, for federated or continual learning, and for transferring inductive biases. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.'}, {'author': 'Murillo', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.'}, {'author': 'Cameron', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models', 'abstract': 'Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.'}, {'author': 'Stewart', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster ones while transferring performance and often additional properties such as robustness or cross-domain adaptability. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.'}, {'author': 'Mayo', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network.
