papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across vision, generation, speech, and NLP tasks, distillation methods transfer logits, intermediate representations, and task-relevant signals; when combined with complementary compression techniques they enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Remaining practical challenges include selecting appropriate teacher signals, handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, and dealing with limited or private data, but a growing toolkit of task-aware, layer-wise, adversarial, and data-aware variants mitigates these issues.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential Tool for Practical Deep Learning — Potentials, Pitfalls, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into indispensable tools for deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained, privacy-sensitive, and latency-critical environments. Across modalities—vision, language, speech, and generation—KD enables smaller or heterogeneous models to approach teacher performance, improves interpretability in specific settings, and reduces communication costs in distributed learning. However, distillation is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher biases, suffer under data heterogeneity, and interact subtly with training practices. Careful choices—selective sample usage, multi- or self-distillation, architectural adapters, annealing strategies, and privacy-aware generative replay—help realize KD's benefits while mitigating its limitations. This paper synthesizes evidence from applied and theoretical work to argue that KD should be treated as a central engineering primitive, accompanied by the practices needed for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. Methods span soft-label supervision, feature- and layer-wise imitation, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but gains depend strongly on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, domain shift, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a flexible set of techniques to compress large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, generative modeling, and structured prediction domains, KD variants — including logit transfer, feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free distillation, and task-specific adaptations — provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, low-precision numerics, pruning and layer skipping, or teacher training tailored to students, distillation yields practical, deployable models applicable to constrained hardware and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become core methods for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers across computer vision, speech, graph-based learning, and NLP. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based teacher-student paradigm into feature- and representation-based distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, online and adversarial schemes, and task-specific adaptations (e.g., for BERT and non-autoregressive translation). Work also addresses robustness, privacy, few-shot compression, and practical efficiency (reduced compute and communication) for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Adaptation, Privacy, and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression recipe: it is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from one set of models to another. KD enables production of compact, fast models that retain much of a larger model's performance, and it can be adapted to address domain shift, limited or private data, modality-specific constraints, and even fairness or robustness objectives. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller or more efficient ones, reducing computational cost and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings. Approaches vary in what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate representations, feature maps, attention or decision-boundary information), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, ensemble distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving setups), and how training data or augmentation is used. Empirical results across computer vision, speech/lipreading, retrieval, translation, reading comprehension, CTR prediction, federated learning, GANs, NAS, and Transformer compression show that appropriate combination of distillation objective, data strategy, and model design can yield large gains in efficiency with modest or no loss in accuracy. Practical factors that shape success include teacher strength and mismatch to the student, the complexity of distilled data, the role of pre-training for compact models, targeted selection or augmentation of distillation samples, and orthogonal compression techniques such as structured pruning.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across vision, generation, speech, and NLP tasks, distillation methods transfer logits, intermediate representations, and task-relevant signals; when combined with complementary compression techniques they enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Remaining practical challenges include selecting appropriate teacher signals, handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, and dealing with limited or private data, but a growing toolkit of task-aware, layer-wise, adversarial, and data-aware variants mitigates these issues.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. KD spans logits- and feature-based transfers, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and task-specific adaptations. Its strengths include enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, improving latency and memory footprints, and supporting privacy- or data-constrained scenarios. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, data availability and mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, architectural alignment, and deployment heterogeneity require complementary techniques and task-aware engineering to realize reliable, robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones into a broad set of methods that address efficiency, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness, fairness, and cross-modal transfer. By moving beyond simple logits matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher schemes, data-free and few-shot settings, and meta-learned teachers, distillation can both preserve performance and add functional guarantees (e.g., robustness, fairness) that are crucial for real-world deployment. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be considered a foundational component of model compression pipelines and of strategies for adapting large pre-trained models to constrained, specialized, or sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.
