papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become core methods for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers across computer vision, speech, graph-based learning, and NLP. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based teacher-student paradigm into feature- and representation-based distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, online and adversarial schemes, and task-specific adaptations (e.g., for BERT and non-autoregressive translation). Work also addresses robustness, privacy, few-shot compression, and practical efficiency (reduced compute and communication) for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable models while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature shows a wide range of KD mechanisms (logit- and feature-based losses, adversarial and data-free schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols) and application domains (NLP, vision, multimodal, detection, federated settings). KD succeeds best when combined with complementary practices—pretraining, layer-wise alignment, data augmentation, teacher adaptation, and hardware-aware compression—but it faces limitations from teacher errors, data absence, distributional mismatch, and heterogeneous deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Methods extend beyond simple teacher-logit matching to include feature and representation alignment, relational objectives, contrastive methods, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling, curriculum and progressive replacement schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware workflows. KD has been successfully applied across vision, language, speech, graph-structured data, retrieval, and constrained-device deployments, and is commonly combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency and memory budgets. Key practical concerns include what to transfer, how to cope with teacher-student mismatch and limited or private data, optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, and measurement of distilled model robustness and fairness. While empirical progress has been large and diverse, theoretical and systems-level problems remain active areas of research.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or specialized students to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use a range of objectives — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational losses, adversarially generated supervision, and teacher-free/self-distillation variants — often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective in many settings (supervised, self-supervised, online, federated, and data-free), but its success depends on choices about what information to transfer, teacher quality and alignment to the student, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and the complement of compression techniques used. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both why distillation helps (regularization, privileged information, smoother targets) and when it struggles (capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena), suggesting hybrid pipelines and task-aware designs as practical routes forward.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer knowledge from larger or more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, faster, or more interpretable students. Over the past decade these approaches have been adapted across modalities and tasks — from image classification and object detection to sequence models and large pretrained language models — and have been combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning and low-precision quantization. Empirical and theoretical work has highlighted both the practical gains of distillation (improved student generalization, reduced latency and memory, enabling deployment) and key limitations (optimization gaps, distribution mismatch, loss of certain types of information). A range of innovations — feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, self-distillation, data-free distillation with generative replay, teacher adaptation, and weighted/importance-aware soft labels — have been proposed to close these gaps and extend KD to settings such as domain adaptation, privacy-preserving federated learning, cross-modal transfer, and low-resource devices.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: What is known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression strategies form a broad, practically driven toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, graph learning, self-supervision, and reinforcement learning—research has developed many algorithmic variants (logit and feature matching, attention/relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes), system-level protocols (federated, black-box, data-free), and architecture-aware methods (task-adaptive compression, neural architecture search, pruning and quantization combinations). Empirically, KD often substantially reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success depends on teacher–student alignment, available data and augmentations, and task-specific design; remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, domain shift, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Practical deployments balance distilled signals, data strategies, and architecture choices to achieve required trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Cross-Domain Argument for Practical, Responsible, and Multi-Modal Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for deploying modern deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across vision, language, graph, and generative domains, distillation methods can preserve most of a teacher's performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication. Best results come from (a) matching appropriate internal representations (layer mapping, attention, many-to-many mappings), (b) designing teachers or multi-teacher schemes that are student-aware, and (c) combining distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, NAS, adversarial training, federated schemes). However, practitioners must be mindful of failure modes—bias amplification, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and gaps when no training data are available—and adopt targeted mitigations such as task-adaptive compression, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, and data-free or privacy-preserving distillation when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to reduce the resource footprint of large neural networks while preserving performance. The literature surveys a range of approaches — from vanilla teacher-student soft-target transfers to layer-wise, attention- and channel-wise methods, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with pruning and adversarial training — and demonstrates successful applications across NLP, speech, vision, graph, and multimodal problems. Empirical results show effective speedups and parameter reductions with modest accuracy loss; theoretical and empirical analyses also connect KD to label-smoothing and regularization effects that can improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade these techniques have diversified from simple logit-matching to a broad set of objectives and pipelines — including feature- and representation-matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial procedures, data-free and privacy-aware methods, multi-teacher schemes, teacher design, and selective sample strategies. KD has been applied across domains (NLP, vision, graph learning, generative models, novel-view synthesis, speech, and recommender systems), producing substantial reductions in parameters and latency while retaining or sometimes improving downstream performance. The literature highlights important practical trade-offs (utility vs. fairness, robustness, data availability, and teacher–student mismatch), and suggests promising directions in adaptive teacher design, rigorous uncertainty and fairness controls, and domain- and task-specific distillation objectives.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable models across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When paired with complementary techniques—layer mapping, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, pruning/quantization, and curriculum or online schemes—KD yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance while supporting privacy-conscious and latency-constrained deployments. Remaining limits around data availability, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional mismatch can be mitigated by choosing appropriate distillation targets and architectures and by combining KD with targeted engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their capabilities. KD enables deployment across modalities and constrained environments, and empirical work shows it can approach teacher performance when combined with complementary techniques. However, KD is not a universal solution: it can propagate teacher errors and biases, struggle under data scarcity or mismatch, and require careful choices of distilled targets, architectures, and training schedules. To realize KD's benefits in production and research settings, practitioners should pair distillation with targeted remedies—representation-aware objectives, data-and-curriculum strategies, ensemble or adversarial schemes, and fairness or privacy interventions—tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A wide variety of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from logits and feature matching to ensemble, adversarial, self- and teacher-free methods—have been developed and successfully applied across machine translation, retrieval, speech, recommendation, vision, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data complexity, and alignment between teacher and student, and it can propagate teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena) unless mitigated by targeted design choices. When combined with data-centric practices (filtering, augmentation), ensemble strategies, intermediate-layer alignment, or complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization), KD provides a robust, broadly applicable framework for achieving favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical framework for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving functionality across modalities. When combined with task-aware choices of distilled signals, data strategies, and complementary compression methods, KD enables large reductions in model size and latency with modest performance loss and can also address privacy, robustness, and deployment constraints. However, KD has failure modes — including propagation of teacher biases, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shifts — that require targeted remedies. Careful design, including multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, exposure to raw or synthesized data, and joint optimization with pruning or architecture search, makes KD an indispensable component of practical model-deployment toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.
