Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Methods extend beyond simple teacher-logit matching to include feature and representation alignment, relational objectives, contrastive methods, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling, curriculum and progressive replacement schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware workflows. KD has been successfully applied across vision, language, speech, graph-structured data, retrieval, and constrained-device deployments, and is commonly combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency and memory budgets. Key practical concerns include what to transfer, how to cope with teacher-student mismatch and limited or private data, optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, and measurement of distilled model robustness and fairness. While empirical progress has been large and diverse, theoretical and systems-level problems remain active areas of research.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. When combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and feature-level objectives, adversarial or relational losses, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, NAS), KD enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss and can sometimes improve generalization. KD also faces clear limits—teacher bias, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and optimization instability—that require task-aware curricula, multi-teacher or ensemble strategies, and careful selection of distilled signals. This paper argues that KD should be the first-line instrument in compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, provided practitioners adopt principled protocols that address known failure modes and integrate KD with complementary methods for the target deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: The Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains. KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and progressive replacement to yield compact models that preserve much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, teacher quality, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Addressing pitfalls such as harmful teacher supervision on particular samples, degraded signals for low-frequency outputs, data unavailability, privacy concerns, and fairness requires targeted strategies (selective distillation, adapted teachers, self-distillation, generative replay, or tailored objectives).

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have evolved from a simple teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a broad toolbox for producing compact, efficient, and adaptable models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research has produced a range of practical methods—logit and feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware variants, and federated or online protocols—and has clarified connections to regularization, ensemble learning, and optimization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of the teacher's performance, though gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and adaptation to deployment constraints. This synthesis summarizes core methods, theoretical insights, empirical findings, practical considerations, and open challenges that shape current best practice for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and federative settings, distillation can preserve much of a teacher's predictive quality while reducing inference latency, memory footprint, and communication costs. Different distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, contrastive signals) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot) make KD adaptable to diverse deployment constraints. At the same time, distillation has well-documented failure modes—transfer of teacher biases, degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena, sensitivity to data heterogeneity and teacher–student capacity mismatch—and practical success depends on task-aware design choices and often combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. The field thus treats KD as a multifaceted, application-driven set of methods whose best practice is to match signals, data, and student capacity to deployment needs while applying targeted mitigations for privacy, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Universal Tool for Model Compression and Practical Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique that enables model compression, deployment efficiency, and task- or domain-specific adaptation across a wide range of deep learning settings. Empirical work shows KD can reduce memory and compute with small accuracy loss, enable low-precision inference, compress specialized generative or multi-modal models, and provide routes to interpretability and data- or privacy-constrained scenarios. Best results arise when KD is adapted to the task (choice of objectives, teacher ensembles, data augmentation, or data-free strategies) and when student architectures or training protocols explicitly account for heterogeneity between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Hamilton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to the task, available data, and student capacity, KD can deliver substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving most of the teacher's performance. Success depends on selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, annealing), and how to handle limited or private data (data-free synthesis, adversarial generators, teacher-free regularizers). Although KD is broadly effective, it is not a panacea: failures arise from teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, optimization issues, and transferred biases, motivating targeted protocols and continued research into privacy-aware, robust, and automated distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a flexible set of techniques to compress large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, generative modeling, and structured prediction domains, KD variants — including logit transfer, feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free distillation, and task-specific adaptations — provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, low-precision numerics, pruning and layer skipping, or teacher training tailored to students, distillation yields practical, deployable models applicable to constrained hardware and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative modeling, researchers transfer information via softened output distributions, intermediate-feature matching, relational and attention maps, and many-to-many layer alignment. Variants address resource heterogeneity, data unavailability, privacy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical and analytic work shows that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, but its success depends on design choices (what to transfer, teacher quality, data or pseudo-data, and alignment losses). State-of-the-art practice mixes logits-based loss with feature- or representation-level objectives, task-aware augmentations, and architecture- or training-aware modifications to obtain favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in deployment.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from teacher models. Across tasks and modalities, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and structure-preserving objectives—enable deployable models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory use, and communication cost. Distillation also serves as a flexible substrate for addressing domain adaptation, lifelong learning, robustness, low-precision deployment, and generator compression. However, realizing these benefits in practice requires careful design choices around what to transfer, how to map layers and representations, how to handle limited or private teacher data, and how to mitigate bias or robustness loss.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal systems, and specialized domains such as healthcare and novel-view synthesis, KD yields large reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher performance when applied with task-aware design choices. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what information is transferred (logits, features, relational structure), the availability and nature of data, teacher quality and design, and careful integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Pragmatic deployment requires attention to robustness, bias propagation, data scarcity, and domain mismatch, and benefits most from combining KD with task- and hardware-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are no longer just ways to reduce parameter counts; when designed thoughtfully they preserve or even improve task performance, domain robustness, and privacy while enabling real-time deployment. Effective distillation requires going beyond matching output probabilities: transferring internal representations, using task- and domain-aware selection of teacher signals, leveraging ensemble or adversarial schemes when appropriate, and adopting data-aware or data-free augmentation techniques. In application domains from NLP to vision, multi-modal systems, and graph learning, tailored distillation strategies yield substantial speedups and parameter reductions with minimal loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy. This paper synthesizes evidence across diverse recent works to advocate a principled, task-centered approach to distillation and compression.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from teacher models. Across tasks and modalities, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and structure-preserving objectives—enable deployable models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory use, and communication cost. Distillation also serves as a flexible substrate for addressing domain adaptation, lifelong learning, robustness, low-precision deployment, and generator compression. However, realizing these benefits in practice requires careful design choices around what to transfer, how to map layers and representations, how to handle limited or private teacher data, and how to mitigate bias or robustness loss.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Benefits, Practical Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD enables deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints, and can be adapted for task-specific compression, federated and data-free settings, low-precision inference, and bias- or domain-aware transfer. However, KD also carries practical limits: optimization gaps that prevent perfect teacher matching, transfer of teacher biases, failures on low-frequency phenomena, and sensitivity to data availability and teacher-student compatibility. To realize KD's promise practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, relations), consider multi-teacher and confidence-weighting schemes, leverage task-aware architecture search when appropriate, and adopt specialized strategies (data-free generation, reverse distillation, counterfactual augmentation, or federated protocols) to address specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are essential for deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints. Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and NLP shows that combining sensible pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals (outputs and internal representations), appropriate training data or augmentation, and dynamic teacher-student strategies yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Complementary techniques — online or mutual distillation, data-free and federated distillation, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation — further extend applicability to privacy-constrained, multi-domain, and large-scale training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers, ensembles, or supernets) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, distillation strategies include matching logits, mimicking intermediate features, adversarial generation of surrogate data, ensemble compression, and teacher-student co-training. Practical extensions address limited or private data, multi-teacher and domain-shift scenarios, and architecture search for generative models. Empirical results show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, pretraining of compact models, and task-aware feature imitation can preserve much of the teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, and that specialized methods are required for structured outputs (e.g., detection, segmentation, ranking) and domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, widely used toolbox to transfer behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, resource-efficient students. The approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or generated samples), whether original training data are available, and whether the objective emphasizes efficiency, privacy, robustness, or interpretability. Across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives and training pipelines—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—produce compact models that approach teacher performance under deployment constraints. Key practical challenges are capacity and optimization mismatch between teacher and student, data- and privacy-limited settings, distribution shift and low-frequency phenomena, and the risk of transferring undesirable teacher traits; promising responses include task-aware filtering of teacher signals, multi-layer mapping strategies, data-free sample synthesis, and privacy-preserving noise mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.
